reasoning: The underlying problem — flagged AI actions executing before human review when monitors outpace reviewer capacity — is explicitly recognized and partially formalized in recent AI control work. "Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments" (arXiv 2512.22154, Dec 2025) frames oversight latency, actions awaiting review, parallel instances, and even derives a semi-synchronous availability formula 1/(1+λpτ) tying action rate λ, false-positive rate p, and audit duration τ — but it treats τ as a fixed constant and explicitly does NOT model reviewer capacity as a queue or produce staffing guidance. The AI Control / Control Tax line (2312.06942, 2409.07985, 2506.05296) handles human auditing as a static fraction-of-traffic budget with threshold-from-FPR, not as dynamic M/M/c backlog. Queueing theory for human+AI review exists ("Queue & AI," arXiv 2605.27202) but targets workflow productivity/rework, not the safety question of unreviewed execution of a flagged action. The proposal's specific queue-theoretic staffing/threshold-curve angle sits in a genuine gap, but it is a fairly direct extension of an already-published formula and a recognized open problem, so it is partially addressed rather than novel.

evidence.title: Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments
evidence.summary: Directly frames the proposal's problem: oversight latency, actions flagged by monitors awaiting human review, parallel agent instances, and a safety-latency tradeoff across synchronous/semi-synchronous/asynchronous monitoring. Derives a semi-synchronous availability formula 1/(1+lambda*p*tau) linking action rate, FPR, and audit duration. Crucially treats review time tau as a FIXED constant and does NOT use queueing theory or model reviewer capacity/backlog, and provides no staffing or threshold guidance curves — leaving exactly the gap the proposal targets.

evidence.title: Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check
evidence.summary: Models AI control auditing/monitoring overhead, monitor ROC curves, and resource-constrained auditing via suspiciousness thresholds with a human audit budget. Treats audit capacity as a static fraction-of-traffic budget rather than a dynamic queue with c servers; does not derive probability of unreviewed execution from queue dynamics or staffing levels.

evidence.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
evidence.summary: Foundational AI control paper establishing that monitor thresholds must be calibrated to limited human audit capacity (e.g. ~2% of traffic). Establishes the FPR-vs-audit-capacity relationship the proposal builds on, but uses a static auditing budget abstraction, not a queueing/staffing throughput model.

evidence.title: Queue & AI: When Faster Tasks Slow Down the Workflow
evidence.summary: Applies queueing theory (arrival processes, service-time variance, congestion-dependent review thresholds) to AI-assisted human workflows. Demonstrates the proposed method is viable in an adjacent domain, but its objective is workflow productivity and rework dynamics, NOT the AI-safety question of the probability a flagged risky action executes before audit completes.

evidence.title: OR Practice — A Queueing Model for Telephone Operator Staffing
evidence.summary: Representative classic operations-research queueing/staffing work (M/M/c, square-root staffing). Confirms the analytical method is mature and standard, but the structured-DB searches surfaced no work connecting such queueing-staffing models to AI control monitoring or to probability of unreviewed execution of monitor-flagged actions.
